title: The History of Fake Towns.
summary: Josh and Chuck explore fake cities built throughout history. They open with a plug for colleagues' book and tour dates, then cover the Potemkin village legend, the North Korean propaganda village near the DMZ, and the Nazi-staged Theresienstadt camp shown to the Red Cross. Next are World War II decoy cities in Britain (Starfish sites, which diverted bombers and reportedly saved lives), the Paris replica decoy from World War One, and Boeing's disguised fake suburb over its Seattle B-17 plant. They then discuss the APIX town in Palm Beach County tied to a liquid hydrogen rocket fuel plant, and paper towns and trap streets, especially Agloe, New York. Next is weapons testing: Nevada test site mock towns, the Japanese Project Ichiban village, and the University of Michigan's M City driverless car town. They also cover the proposed Center for Innovation, Testing and Evaluation (C-ITE) future city, the Arrow Jet missile silo, police and military training villages, and the 1960s Riotsville sites, which they plan to revisit. The episode ends with a listener mail about stereo vinyl mid-side encoding and a sign-off.

entities.name: Center for Innovation, Testing and Evaluation

segments.title: Opening banter and live show plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck plug upcoming live shows in Seattle, Portland and San Francisco and a colleagues' book, then introduce the topic of fake cities such as the Blazing Saddles town of Rock Ridge.

segments.title: Potemkin villages and North Korea
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Potemkin village legend, which is now a term for fake facades used as propaganda, and the North Korean propaganda village visible from the DMZ.

segments.title: Theresienstadt Nazi staged town
segments.summary: The Nazis cleaned up and staged a camp depot for a Red Cross visit, presenting it as a spa town. The hosts say the deception worked and that it was known only from postwar history.

segments.title: WWII British decoy sites and Starfish cities
segments.summary: British decoy sites called Starfish sites, or special fire sites, were built to draw German bombers away from real cities. The hosts say 237 sites diverted about 700 raids and potentially saved about 3,000 lives. Colonel John Turner is credited with the idea.

segments.title: Paris WWI zeppelin decoy
segments.summary: During World War One the French planned a life-size decoy replica of Paris to counter zeppelin raids. Only the industrial section was completed, and the plan was dropped when the zeppelin threat faded.

segments.title: Boeing's disguised Seattle plant town
segments.summary: Boeing hid its B-17 plant in Seattle under a fake suburb built on top of the factory. Workers were sent up to lend the illusion of normal life, and the street grid was aligned to match the real area.

segments.title: APIX town and paper towns / Agloe
segments.summary: The hosts describe the APIX worker town in Palm Beach County, tied to a liquid hydrogen rocket fuel plant, and its name's origin. They then cover paper towns and trap streets, focusing on Agloe, New York, which became real after a fishing lodge and general store adopted the name, and a Rand McNally lawsuit.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break with a short mid-episode transition.

segments.title: Weapons testing towns and M City
segments.summary: Fake towns built for nuclear weapons testing at the Nevada Test Site, including the house that survived and the mannequins; Japan's Project Ichiban village; and the University of Michigan's M City, a fake town used to test driverless cars.

segments.title: C-ITE future city, Arrow Jet silo, and police training villages
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the proposed Center for Innovation, Testing and Evaluation future city, the Arrow Jet missile silo in Dade County, military and police training villages, and Riotsville, which they plan to cover in a future episode.

segments.title: Listener mail on vinyl stereo
segments.summary: Marcus writes that stereo records use mid-side encoding, which the hosts discuss. They also address listener criticism of earlier episodes and read out the contact address.
